title: Key changes in tunes keep rhythmic playing fresh
summary: Ashcraft explains how China Boy and New Orleans tunes modulate, giving new life to each chorus.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Uh, did they ever get to the point, well, this, I, uh, is a loaded question. Uh, where they, it became, uh, rhythmically monotonous. Now, the rock and roll, uh, calls for a very pronounced beat. And it can be a 4-4 or 2-4. And, uh, after a while, you kind of wish it would ever.

Well, there's something in the nature of the tunes they were playing. I mentioned China Boy, for instance. Uh, the Wolverines used to play it quite a lot because that was a standard tune they played when, uh, they were requested to play something they didn't know. Oh. If somebody, uh, it was very fashionable. Uh, it took six months for a show tune to get from New York to Chicago. Uh-huh. At that stage. And anybody who'd been in New York was very proud of being from New York. So they would always request the show tune they'd heard while they were there. Uh, so if somebody asked for a Gershwin tune, the Wolverines played China Boy. But getting back to the point, uh, China Boy changes from F to A flat in the release. It's a whole new life to it, the tune. Well, so are all the other rhythm tunes. Uh, uh, Muskrat or any of the tunes like, um, Tiger Rag, for instance, that go right through the progression of keys. And most of the New Orleans tunes did. They'd be, uh, A flat, E flat. Uh, I mean, uh, B flat, E flat, A flat. You see? And progress. Well, as you rise in those, in those keys, it's a new life, sort of.
The rock and roll guys do the same thing in their shift up of a half tone for the next chorus. They're trying to do that.
